question: to the Commission Dan-Ştefan Motreanu (PPE) Subject:

In the light of increased cooperation between Member States’ enforcement authorities and non-EU countries, including the United Kingdom, Ukraine and Canada, the Commission recently announced its aim to extend the scope of the Prüm II Regulation1. The regulation provides a framework for the automated exchange of biometric and identification data between Member States, and the Commission now seeks to bring non-EU countries within its scope in order to combat the fragmentation that might arise from the current approach. Therefore, given that non-EU countries are not subject to the same data protection standards as the EU Member States, what measures is the Commission exploring to ensure that data exchanges under the extended framework meet an adequate level of protection?

Regulation (EU) 2024/982 of 13 March 2024 on the automated search and exchange of data for police cooperation, and amending Council Decisions 2008/615/JHA and 2008/616/JHA and Regulations (EU) 2018/1726, (EU) No 2019/817 and (EU) 2019/818 of the European Parliament and of the Council (the Prüm II Regulation) (OJ L, 2024/982, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/982/oj). 1
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.8.2026) The so-called Prüm International initiative aims at strengthening information exchange for law enforcement purposes with key trusted non-EU countries. The Commission will explore the measures available under EU law for such exchanges, as indicated also in the call for evidence1. Directive (EU) 2016/6802 applies to exchange of data between competent authorities of Member States for the purposes of prevention, investigation, detection or prosecution of criminal offences or execution of criminal penalties. The Directive also provides for specific measures concerning the transfer of personal data to third countries, particularly the existence of an adequacy decision with the third country (Article 36) or appropriate safeguards (Article 37). With the Prüm International initiative, the Commission will aim to ensure that the information exchange for law enforcement purposes with key trusted non-EU countries will meet high EU standards on data security and fundamental rights, including data protection, with clear purpose limitation and national oversight over operational decisions.
